items.title: Tumbly: An Open-Source Home-Cage Device for Time-Restricted Feeding in Mice
items.summary: Preprint describing Tumbly, a battery-powered, servo-driven food hopper that gates diet access on a user-set schedule and fits multiple vivarium cage types via a swappable faceplate; design files are open. Validation in two labs reported no device failures over >1000 hours and normal body weight and intake under 8-h TRF.

details.hub_relevance: Directly overlaps the Hub's automated feeding, circadian, and battery-powered home-cage device lines and could pair with Hublink-style cloud logging.

items.title: Cortex-wide imaging in naturally behaving mice with 1-gram wireless mesoscopes (Airscope)
items.summary: Tsinghua University researchers report Airscope, a fully wireless ~1 g head-mounted mesoscope (including battery) with a ~6 mm field of view that streams cortex-wide calcium imaging over Wi-Fi from freely behaving mice. The paper reports recording more than 8,500 neurons per mouse and simultaneous multi-animal recording.

details.hub_relevance: Battery-powered wireless head-mounted recording in freely moving, socially housed mice parallels the Hub's low-power wireless wearable work (Juxta, BEAM3) and its optical instrumentation interests.

items.title: Camus: a video-based framework for continuous behavioral monitoring in the mouse home-cage
items.summary: Preprint presenting Camus, an open-source home-cage video system using off-the-shelf USB cameras, IR illumination, and 3D-printed parts with a validated computer-vision model for locomotion, feeding, drinking, and nesting. One desktop records up to 20 cages at ~$250 incremental cost per cage and captured circadian structure and 5xFAD nesting deficits.

details.hub_relevance: Provides a low-cost video ground truth for the same circadian home-cage behaviors the Hub measures with BEAM3, Hub Wheel, and FlightCap sensors.

items.title: Individual-level data in group-housed home-cage monitoring
items.summary: Survey users rank group housing among their biggest constraints. Open-source PIR systems such as RAD and MIROSLAV can't tell group-housed animals apart and only detect overall locomotion. Video systems are costly or need special enclosures. Juxta already records proximity, temperature, and movement for each animal for up to a month.

details.potential_value: Strategic: puts the Hub in a recognized, underserved niche (social behavior plus welfare and the 3Rs). Buyers are behavioral neuroscience, pharmacology, and animal-welfare labs.
details.recommended_action: Low-cost interest test via waitlist/landing page and user interviews

items.title: Scheduled, logged, weatherproof playback for unattended field playback experiments
items.summary: Playback experiments are a core field-ecology method, but requiring a human present disrupts behavior and limits sample size (BoomBox, Methods Ecol Evol). The leading open option, BoomBox (~$75), is trigger-only with ~15 min of MP3 audio. ACORN adds scheduled/random daily programs, IP65 housing, ~103 dB output, and CSV environment logs. The gap is partly validated (need is documented); demand at ACORN's $799 price is a hypothesis.
